items.question: How do you understand the Alberta Plan as an approach to pursuing artificial general intelligence?
items.object: The Alberta Plan
items.answer: The Alberta plan is an approach to pursuing really strong artificial general intelligence, which has deep roots. It's something that I think a lot of us at the University of Alberta and at the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, and its precursor, the AICL, have pursued over the years. It is both a structure for how we might think about building intelligent agents that can learn from their own experience and a set of commitments that tie us to an approach to doing research which we believe is going to be able to support generating these kinds of new future technologies.

items.question: How do you see the role of artificial intelligence in your lab's work on bionic medicine?
items.object: Artificial intelligence in bionic medicine and prosthetic restoration
items.answer: I'm currently working mostly in bionic medicine, artificial intelligence applied to how humans and machines interact. In particular, our research lab is working on a very cool, I think very ambitious, research project where we're looking at literally bolting robots into the bones of the human body. We work on artificial intelligence and transformative surgeries and ways of measuring people's interactions with prostheses. We're looking at people with amputation or other forms of limb difference, and how we might begin to build a new sort of science and art of prosthetic restoration, neuroprostheses for people who use artificial arms and hands in particular. We're looking at bone-anchoring surgeries, how you can rewire the human nervous system to engage better with a decision-making machine, like an artificial limb or hand, and then building a new generation of artificial intelligence technologies that glue that person and machine together in an informational sense, to act as a broker to translate what the human wants into what the artificial limb is actually able to deliver. We're working on bionic medicine. It's very, very cool. What I think—how this ties into our conversation today—is that it's an example of machine learning technologies, reinforcement technologies, that are deployed in very low-compute environments. We're not imagining an artificial limb that continually talks to a supercomputer in space every time it wants to try to open and close a hand. We want devices that people can wear on or attach to their body.

items.object: The Alberta Plan as a research program for artificial general intelligence
items.answer: The Alberta plan is an approach to pursuing really strong artificial general intelligence, which has deep roots. items.question: How do you think learning and acting should relate over an agent's lifetime in the Alberta Plan?
items.object: Continuous learning from experience in the Alberta Plan
items.answer: One is that it's very experience-based: we believe in agents that are living within the flow of time. Another commitment is that there isn't really temporal uniformity. There's no special training and testing period. We're not taking a billion dollars to distill down all of Reddit plus the rest of the internet and turn it into a model. The idea in the Alberta plan is that all of the data that flows into the system, that stream of experience, the agent living within its stream of experience, is always being incrementally added to what it already knows. We're not trying to divide up time into epochs of batches of learning versus batches of acting. Acting and learning are dovetailed together in an inseparable way.

items.question: Why do you place such importance on computational efficiency in the Alberta Plan?
items.object: Computational efficiency in the Alberta Plan
items.answer: In the Alberta plan we talk a lot about respecting computation, respecting every one of those FLOPs we're using. Every single act of computation should be valuable. If we can be as computationally efficient as possible in how we think about the learning process, then we can do more learning. Imagine a bunny rabbit hopping through the briar bushes. If you make its operation more efficient, it can predict more things about its environment. It can start to build up expectations about its world in a way that we couldn't otherwise.

items.question: What makes the Alberta Plan's commitment to studying other agents especially compelling to you?
items.object: Multi-agent interactions and intelligence amplification in the Alberta Plan
items.answer: The last thing we want to observe and commit to studying in the Alberta plan is the idea that there are other agents in the world. Whether or not an agent, a learning machine, has to identify, codify, or build an explicit representation for another agent that lives in the world with it, other agents in the world create complexity, create patterns that are learnable, and create richness in the environment, as well as the potential to amplify the capacity of a decision-making agent. This is the bit of the Alberta plan I'm perhaps most passionate about: the longstanding idea of intelligence amplification, going right back to Ashby in the 1950s and the post-cyberneticists, and thinking about the ability to directly paraphrase Ashby: intelligence, much like physical ability, might be amplified by tools that we can use. We can use one intelligence to multiply the abilities of another, and artificial intelligence and computation are powerful amplifiers we might have. That last commitment of the Alberta plan, which I hold pretty near and dear, is very much that we might start to see the ability of intelligence to multiply the capacity of other intelligences.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between an intelligent agent and its environment?
items.object: The boundary and interaction between an intelligent agent and its environment
items.answer:
I think it's a very flexible line that separates the agent and the environment. I think it's a very deliberate choice. If I was an industrial process designer, I would be very deliberate at choosing where that interface is. If I was a thinking machine trying to live its life in its flow of experience, that dotted line might change over time. What's interesting about the separation of the agent and the environment is that it necessitates a relationship between them. We have to assume that the agent's learning is going to be with respect to what a number of people call the aperture between the agent and the world. That's a fundamental piece of the equation.

We're able to create machines that are able to hold in their digital minds the sum total of the internet and all these private data islands attached to it. This is miraculous. I don't want to trivialize that. But the relationship between an agent and its environment is special. If we truly want to build thinking machines that can live within their flow of experience, whatever their world is—whether it's the world of protocol buffers flowing between data centers or the human world of desks, tables, chairs, and doors—we have to deeply consider that interaction between the agent and the environment. That's part of its learning.

Another piece of that is the body, whatever it is, whether it's some kind of network router or a protocol buffer or a piece of metal moving itself through the world. There is physical intelligence within that system. Rodney Brooks has had amazing long discussions about this and has written quite eloquently about how the physical intelligence, the way the body itself not just translates the intelligence of whatever the mind is, but in fact contains some aspects of intelligence itself. This necessitates our consideration of the environment.

That's not to say that we can't have an agent that watches a ton of YouTube videos and then is able to go out there and interact with the world itself—but if we want agents that not only can interact with the world but can continue to adapt to worlds and new worlds that they encounter, it's very important that we think about the environment. The representations we choose, the data streams that we integrate into agent learning, are absolutely critical. This is the perspective we take, the Alberta plan perspective: what is being learned is about that aperture between the agent and the environment.

items.question: How do you see pretrained foundation models fitting into an agent's learning from its own experience?
items.object: Models learned from an agent's own experience and their compatibility with pretrained foundation models
items.answer:
What's cool is that what is learned can take many forms. We often think about value functions. We think about expectations about the future that are about a signal of interest, or many different signals of interest. Those can then be used to sculpt behavior. Those forecasts an agent makes, the way that the agent starts to build up expectations about its future experience, might be about that cool signal we call reward. We love reward. It's a nice, precious, very good signal. There's a reward signal going through the agent-environment loop, too, but there are all these other things to learn.

When I think about model, I think about something an animal or machine agent has formed that is able to carry the likeness of something, in this case mostly its environment and interactions with its environment. That's a very big-tent approach to model, but I do think about this sort of internal construct which allows an agent to represent, manipulate, improve its computation, and leverage its experience about the world to choose and make actions. If we have that model, the nice thing is, could we put in a large pre-trained model, something we'd call a foundation model? You could absolutely leverage something like that.

We can imagine permissive models that take into account all sorts of expectations about the world, all sorts of ways of representing the world and the way streams of experience might unfold in that world. We could admit things that have been learned that were not learned directly by an agent. I think that's okay. We can also admit into our definition of models, and how an agent might use it to improve its action and its computation, models that are learned directly from its raw experience. I think, speaking for myself and my colleagues as well, that area, learning from its raw experience and unlocking its true potential, is underexplored comparatively speaking, and has great power. That's something we would want to continue to reinforce: reinforcement learning is able to build up this understanding of an agent's interactions with its world.

The reinforcement learning agent is going to build up forecasts about its future from its raw sensory motor experience. That's really critical, but it's compatible with other kinds of models that might be learned. That could be the YouTube-watching agent: 'I watched a bunch of robots and video games, all the speedruns I could see, and now I'm going to use that to inform my motor control.' That's totally okay. I like that. I think that just makes sense.

items.question: Why do you favor agents that learn predictive models from raw experience?
items.object: Predictive models learned from an agent's raw experience
items.answer: Of the kind of models I like, I really like considering agents that have predictive models of their world. This means the kind of model they might form is about the raw bits of experience flowing across all of those wires into their digital mind. For years I've taken what normal engineers would say were perfectly reasonable signals, like the joint angle of a finger, the current going into a servo motor, or the pressure, and taken those perfectly reasonable scalar floating-point numbers and just turned them into bits and stuffed those bits into the mind of the agent so it can start to predict the future of how those bits are going to change. My default perspective is very much blinking lights on wires: the agent is predicting its raw experience without that experience being tagged or labeled or even separated into bins that we might call a floating-point number or an eight-bit integer. I love predictive models. I think agents that leverage their predictive models have amazing potential to interact with diverse environments in ways that agents that are structurally biased by our human way of segmenting the world might be limited.

items.question: What do you find powerful about the 'Reward Is Enough' idea from David Silver, Satinder Singh, and Rich Sutton?
items.object: The 'Reward Is Enough' idea and reinforcement learning's role in developing capabilities
items.answer: The idea that you might use reinforcement learning to take whatever kind of base understanding—the ability to act or make decisions, produce tokens, or produce motor trajectories—and place reinforcement learning within that to sculpt and optimize or adapt that behavior feels absolutely right. I think we probably see this happening in biology all the time. You mentioned DeepSeek. That's another great example. We were discussing this at a reading group yesterday. We brought in the paper from David Silver, Satinder Singh, and Rich Sutton called 'Reward Is Enough.' To paraphrase poorly what our colleague said in that paper: if you have a single signal of reward, this precious signal, and an agent is truly trying to maximize the extended amount of that signal it collects over time, and the task requires it to learn anything from chain-of-thought reasoning or social interaction or vision, then if the task requires the agent to build this advanced capacity—simple or advanced capacity of what we consider intelligence—that signal of reward is enough to drive the agent to create whatever it is. For the DeepSeek paper, this is the idea that it might start to create chains of reasoning, that it might be able to unfold in its little think brackets the steps it took to get to a solution, and then the reward signal itself from all those myriad tasks is driving the creation of those chains of reasoning, outside of other labeled examples being stuffed in, of course compatible with input information from elsewhere. The 'reward is enough' idea is powerful because it lets us think about how we might close the gap between all those thinking machines that we have created, with thinking that could be very simple or very powerful, and the complete cohort of goals we might have for the technology that surrounds us in our lives. If there's this missing piece—I'd love chain-of-thought reasoning, or social intelligence is going to be really important, or I'd like a better idea of how bio-signals flow from the human body to a robotic device attached to that body—reinforcement learning is perhaps the thing that can pull those two together.

items.question: How do you understand learning about the world through predictions from an agent's own frame of reference?
items.object: Learning about the world through predictions from an agent's own frame of reference
items.answer:
I'll go back to a conversation I think must have been in 2009, when Rich and I were having a conversation about chairs and how you think about chairs and how a machine might think about chairs. The normal way we might think about a chair, or hope a machine thinks about a chair, is to look at the vast swath of computer vision literature that has considered objects like chairs, tables, and doors. You might think about the chair as: How wide is it? How tall is it? Where's the seat? Is the seat hard or soft? How far is the chair from the door? That's a very normal, objective worldview, thinking from the perspective or frame of reference of the world: How do I define the chair, its extrema, its boundaries, its properties? There's another view, the view I think Rich was advocating during that conversation. What's the probability that if I were to try to sit down right now, I would actually sit, or would I fall? If I were to walk three steps, would I bump into something with my shins? There are these very subjective questions from the agent's frame of reference, inside the agent, with respect to the data stream accessible to the agent: What do its predictions say about its interactions with the world around it?

A lot of early sensory motor learning—you look at motor babbling in babies—they start to learn to move their head around and their eyeballs, and figure out that if I move my head this way or that way, there's a noticeable change in my sensory experience. I predict that if I'm able to do this, I'm going to be able to see the ball that's outside my vision. Everything from object permanence to work by Frazier on robots doing the same thing babies do—there's a fantastic paper from quite a few years back. It's neat because the system is beginning to make elegant scientific tests: the agent as a scientist, saying, 'Every time I've moved my head this way, I start to see this other thing,' or 'If I move all of these bits of myself, something appears in front of my face. It's my own hand. Oh, that's so cool.' There's a rudimentary, fundamental learning process that unfolds. You see it with baby animals, humans, and otherwise.

There's a whole cohort of neuroscience literature saying the fact that I feel like I'm moving my arm is not the sensors reporting back that I'm moving my arm. It is my predictions about my arm's movement. If something gets in the way, then there's correction that happens with predictions. The feeling of agency even over my own movements might be due to the predictions in my mind. 'Prediction precedes control,' says Daniel Wolpert and colleagues, in motor learning. From that perspective, you can imagine chaining together all of that process of learning to say you should be able to learn everything you possibly need to know about the world just from signals of reward and predictions of your raw sensory motor behavior. This is the prediction perspective, the subjective agent-frame prediction.

There are these very subjective questions from the agent's frame of reference, inside the agent, with respect to the data stream accessible to the agent: What do its predictions say about its interactions with the world around it?

A lot of early sensory motor learning—you look at motor babbling in babies—they start to learn to move their head around and their eyeballs, and figure out that if I move my head this way or that way, there's a noticeable change in my sensory experience. I predict that if I'm able to do this, I'm going to be able to see the ball that's outside my vision. Everything from object permanence to work by Frazier on robots doing the same thing babies do—there's a fantastic paper from quite a few years back. It's neat because the system is beginning to make elegant scientific tests: the agent as a scientist, saying, 'Every time I've moved my head this way, I start to see this other thing,' or 'If I move all of these bits of myself, something appears in front of my face. It's my own hand. Oh, that's so cool.' There's a rudimentary, fundamental learning process that unfolds. You see it with baby animals, humans, and otherwise.

There's a whole cohort of neuroscience literature saying the fact that I feel like I'm moving my arm is not the sensors reporting back that I'm moving my arm. It is my predictions about my arm's movement. If something gets in the way, then there's correction that happens with predictions. The feeling of agency even over my own movements might be due to the predictions in my mind. 'Prediction precedes control,' says Daniel Wolpert and colleagues, in motor learning. From that perspective, you can imagine chaining together all of that process of learning to say you should be able to learn everything you possibly need to know about the world just from signals of reward and predictions of your raw sensory motor behavior. This is the prediction perspective, the subjective agent-frame prediction.

items.question: What value do you see in pursuing AI that learns from raw sensory motor experience alongside pretrained foundation models?
items.object: Learning from raw sensory motor experience as an alternative foundation for AI
items.answer:
Is that the fastest way to build a robot butler or a self-driving car? Probably not, let's be honest. If I was going to go out and start building a self-driving car right now—I once pitched this to someone: 'Hey, I would happily help your company build a self-driving car. Give me some cars and let me start smashing them into stuff.' They actually said maybe, which I thought was a really positive sign. If you wanted to take the constructivist view, the subjective agent-frame constructivist view of learning a very hard task, like self-driving or full problem-solving at the Math Olympiad, there might be easier or harder ways.

What's neat, though, is if we look at the trajectory of AlphaGo. Everyone loves talking about AlphaGo. I also love talking about the Go board right here. If we think about a version of AlphaGo that learned from watching human examples and then had gaps in its mind's eye, certain delusions, and then go to an AlphaZero which learned through self-play, it was able to drop some of those data biases that let it find solutions it never would have found otherwise. I said earlier, I love having a machine see the world through its raw bits without me even putting floating-point numbers on top of it. Part of that is saying that the agent learning from as raw a sensory motor signal stream as possible allows it to undo some assumptions I might be making as a designer, which means it might be able to find a much better solution, maybe even faster than the other way around.

Building up human language takes a while. For a human to learn human language through trial and error, through motor babbling, is going to take a while. Would we rather juice the internet, make some amazing lemonade, and use that as our foundation model? Large language model, pre-trained, it's great. Of course we would. This makes a lot of sense. Everything everyone is doing makes a lot of sense. But there's this other path. That's why, going back to the Alberta plan, we want to make sure this stays in the public mind's eye: there are alternate and compatible views which allow us to maybe fill in some gaps or start from a very different foundation point. Maybe our current curve goes up and starts to taper off; maybe there's another approach where you pursue this raw sensory motor learning about the stream of experience, but it has a higher final peak. Let's keep that diversity in our mindstream, and not be dogmatic or siloed about it.

items.question: How do you think researchers pursuing raw sensory motor learning should relate to the wider AI research community?
items.object: The relationship between raw sensory motor learning researchers and the wider AI research community
items.answer: I think it's really important that we aren't too siloed or too cliquey in our communities, saying, 'No, I'm going to sit over here and do raw sensory motor learning and ignore everyone else.'

items.question: How do you understand the range of sensory motor and language tasks that reinforcement learning can address?
items.object: Reinforcement learning across sensory motor and language domains
items.answer: I think we're starting to see them, and where we see them most is in specialized, targeted domains. The work from DeepMind on stabilizing plasma in a tokamak reactor: that decision-making system acting thousands of times a second on a very diverse stream of data to literally control a lobe of plasma hotter than the heart of the sun. That's really neat. It's reinforcement learning from reward. Then we see systems that can do elite coding tasks, also driven directly by reward. As we start to see all these different domains, one of those is very sensory motor. I would argue that stabilizing plasma in a tokamak fusion reactor is very much a sensory motor experience. Same thing with cooling a data center or compressing bits in YouTube using MuZero. Those are much more sensory motor, like the nerves firing down the spinal cord and letting my arms do all sorts of cool things. Doing really well at elite coding tasks and programming competitions—reward driving that feels more like language. Reinforcement learning applied in its raw sense can generate insight in both domains.

items.question: What do you find significant about Gran Turismo Sophy's reward-based learning?
items.object: Gran Turismo Sophy and learning social interaction through reward
items.answer: When I give talks I have a 'best of hits' collection at the beginning: 'What's been happening in reinforcement learning? Have you met Gran Turismo Sophy?' Our colleagues at Sony did a really cool job of building a racing system which could do high-performance, superhuman driving while also learning the implicit rules of driving and racing: not cutting people off, not sideswiping people. There are rules of racing it was able to begin to build up, through reward-based learning. Going back to 'Reward Is Enough,' you need some social interaction skills; if the task requires it, you can get that through reward. Do you want to solve a programming task? If you need to think about data structures and how you chain together methods and different computational artifacts, you could drive that with reward.

items.question: How do you think about choosing the fundamental units of an agent's experience?
items.object: The fundamental units of an agent's experience
items.answer: Is it just bits on a wire, like Patrick proposes? Probably not. This is a very bold idea. If we went all the way to thinking about an agent's experience in terms of raw ones and zeros, without any labeling, there's a quick shortcut you can take—which maybe you shouldn't take, if you believe my argument about design biases—and use floating-point numbers and integers. Another option is to use more advanced data structures as the representational, foundational elements that a machine starts to use. You might say it would be faster if we used some of those that we've already learned through supervised learning. A lot of our colleagues would say supervised learning is learning through labeled examples. We learn through trial and error, or from the structure of the data. Each of those might be a great way to start building the fundamental units of experience an agent operates upon. We put out a paper on generalized value functions back in 2011. One reason we were excited about that, and thought about generalizing the idea of learning a value function about reward—expectation of how much reward will I accumulate in the future, assuming I care about the future in this way—to do that for any signal of interest, is that we viewed those predictions, forecasts, and expectations of future signals as foundational elements for building more advanced behaviors for an agent. That goes to the choice of what the fundamental units of an experience stream are.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between Transformer cross-attention and learning a generalized value function?
items.object: The relationship between Transformer cross-attention and generalized value functions
items.answer: I think associations across space and time are very powerful. These systems are able to consider the flow of time, spans of time which are getting increasingly vast, and create associations across that large span of time, but also across different channels of information. It could be anything from the stream of tokens in a sentence alongside audio data coming in, alongside the time series of vision pixels, to the random bits on a wire I was proposing earlier. We have cross-attention, the ability to chain together facets of information in the beautiful gemstone of an agent's past experience to create predictions about the future. Those predictions are acted upon. They're going to move a joint, or more likely spit out a new word token or a new pixel in generative video. The same thing happens in the basic process of learning a generalized value function. Based on a representation of some kind—which we hope can form associations across space and time—a system generates a prediction about the future. These predictions for a generalized value function, for instance, are temporally extended. They might be thinking about the expected sum of a signal conditioned on a policy that assumes some kind of preference over the time window being integrated. Either way, you could definitely do token prediction with that if you wanted to. You can also predict the future condition of a robot arm and start it moving early to catch a ball mid-flight. Associations across different modalities or channels of information, across time, and using that to create a prediction—these are different ways of achieving the same thing. You could imagine using them flexibly together or committing hard to one of them and working on that. I feel like that's the potential here: to see the unity between cross-attention and token prediction in terms of raw sensor experience. There's a lot of unity there that I think we're just not celebrating.

items.question: What excites you about large language models' access to long histories, given your work on incremental learning in the Alberta Plan?
items.object: Large language models' access to long histories and incremental learning in the Alberta Plan
items.answer: I like it because some of the tricks we're starting to see—'tricks' is not to trivialize the elegance of the computation—take a vast history and give access to it. A large language model having access to a vast history of tokens, like me sitting there with Google Gemini and having a lovely conversation about structural neuroscience: there are a lot of tokens going in. We chatted for an hour, and getting these long histories and still thinking about relationships across these vast spans is exciting and new. History is hard. A lot of the work we do for the Alberta plan is about making learning incremental, by making sure that every new sample is bolted onto the old, so we're not keeping around histories.

items.question: How do you prefer to introduce learning into human-facing technologies used in clinical settings?
items.object: Learning systems that begin from and fall back to a gold standard in human-facing technology
items.answer: We've tried a number of different approaches over the years. Maybe I'll say one that continues to shine for me. It works really well in a clinical setting, in an environment where you're trying to bring together technology people who build technology with clinical practitioners who are experts in their clinical fields. I love starting with an approach where the system begins at the gold standard, whatever it is. Especially for human-facing technologies—that's where I mostly work—I would very much like a system that starts at the gold standard and then gets better with experience. It learns through interactions with its raw stream of experience, is able to integrate those other facets of experience into its learning and improve or optimize its behavior from the gold standard, but then falls back to the gold standard if and when it makes a mistake. It still defaults back to whatever that gold-standard operation would be.

items.question: How do you see control theory and reinforcement learning working together in systems that need to adapt to the world?
items.object: The relationship between control theory and reinforcement learning in adaptive systems
items.answer: There are cases, especially human-facing cases, where we want to appeal to control theory. We sure do. Does control theory currently allow us to think hard about soft robotics, deformable systems, a liquid-metal robot able to change its form completely with very strange dynamics, like jamming systems, or other reconfigurable robotic systems? There are branches of control theory attacking those problems, but these are hard problems. There are cases where this piece is definitely going to be nailed by control theory. Can we improve upon it to make it more resilient, agile, and able to adapt to the world around it through learning about its stream of experience? I think the answer is absolutely. RL Core Technologies is a company from Edmonton, and some of our colleagues from the University of Alberta are leading it. They do reinforcement learning technologies. One example is water treatment: you could take a water-treatment system and think about how RL can improve a community's ability to treat water and make sure its drinking water is safe and reliable. There are going to be parts of that which are solid gold-standard control engineering, and then you'll use learning through experience, learning through trial and error, to improve the pieces that can be improved upon that gold standard, so it can adapt to new circumstances and operate for long periods without constant human intervention. These are really space explorations. Another great example: do I want some kind of control system governing my plasma thrusters? I sure do. But do I want the spaceship to steer itself, maybe learn to avoid things in new environments? That would be great. There are certain low-level processes, like the biological processes in our own bodies: the protein machinery in our cells is going about doing its business. There's some adaptation going on there, but a lot of what we think about as intelligence is the thing that's moving around all those little protein machines. Reinforcement learning is learning, right?

items.question: How do you think continual learning should let a system incorporate new experience?
items.object: Continual learning and its two approaches to updating a learning system
items.answer:
A lot of us in the community are passionate about continual learning: a system that is able to continue to learn, adapt, and change. It's very constructive, as in nature. I would hope a system is able to continue to integrate new information into what it knows, not overwrite the old stuff unless the old stuff is supposed to be overwritten, flexibly compose skills and behaviors learned in the past in a new way and in new situations, and continue to do so forever, literally forever.

One approach is: imagine I have a giant large language model with all these factoids baked into it, in whatever way, whether there's a grandmother neuron or a collection of activations that allow us to have the concept of a grandmother. You'd want that system to be incrementally improved without having to go back and spend billions of dollars—or I guess now millions of dollars if you take the DeepSeek approach—to retrain the whole thing from scratch on the data. Maybe you don't want to do that. Maybe you want to take new information and integrate it into that system. My brain—I don't want to retrain my brain every time I learn something new by reading a paper or talking to you today. There's a community looking at that problem, and there have been good advances: taking a piece of information and using it to upgrade an already in-place system.

If we go down to the brass tacks of it, I don't think we have any analog to glial cells in the neuroscience of our digital system, so for the most part we're looking at weights. Can I modify the weights or some other holding-memory variables that are impacting the operation of the network? That's one approach: I'd love continual learning to be a thing. I'd love my large language model to continue to learn. I'd love to take whatever news article popped online, which hopefully isn't also written by a large language model, because then, as we saw from that recent paper, you start to get collapse iterations happening.

The other is that we don't want to just modify a large language model or something. We're thinking about the process, those weights, constantly being updated from raw experience in a very incremental way. That's saying I'm not taking a new factoid and jamming it in; every single moment of interaction is already changing the system. Both views are modifying weights, modifying numbers stored in some kind of digital mind of the machine, but you're hoping they don't overwrite things that shouldn't be overwritten and that they respect context. If I'm upstairs making tea or drinking tea down here, I might want to act differently and think differently about my predictions about the likelihood of spilling hot water on myself.

items.question: Why do you consider long-term stability essential for continual learning systems?
items.object: Long-term stability in continual learning systems
items.answer: Continual learning can happen for long periods. There was a very nice paper by some of our University of Alberta colleagues that showed ways to think about stable continual learning. That paper came out recently and says we have new ways to allow a system to continually keep changing its weights without catastrophic forgetting or catastrophic failure after hundreds of millions of epochs of learning or time steps. You want systems to stay stable for very long periods. If I send out a continual learning system on a spacecraft going to Alpha Centauri, I sure hope we don't find out after 100 million time steps that everything flatlines and it predicts zero for every outcome. There goes your spaceship.

That paper came out recently and says we have new ways to allow a system to continually keep changing its weights without catastrophic forgetting or catastrophic failure after hundreds of millions of epochs of learning or time steps. You want systems to stay stable for very long periods. If I send out a continual learning system on a spacecraft going to Alpha Centauri, I sure hope we don't find out after 100 million time steps that everything flatlines and it predicts zero for every outcome. There goes your spaceship.

items.question: What assumption about neural-network architecture underlies the continual-learning approaches you’ve been describing?
items.object: The fixed-architecture assumption in continual-learning approaches
items.answer: The two examples I was just pitching are both assuming that the network architecture itself stays the same. You have all of the pieces of the network more or less the same shape and size throughout the course of learning, and then you're thinking about how to modify those.
quotes: the two examples I was just pitching are both assuming that the network architecture itself stays the same:

items.question: How do you think about growing a neural network's architecture as part of continual learning?
items.object: Growing neural network architecture as part of continual learning
items.answer: There's a very reasonable, natural approach you might consider. This is a separate piece of continual learning. One approach is we've got a skeleton and we're thinking about how beefy the muscles are in different parts of the skeleton. The other is let's add more bones onto the skeleton and grow muscles around them, the weights being the muscles and the skeleton being the architecture connections. I feel like that's really interesting. There are deep lines of thinking on this; this isn't something we just figured out this year. Respecting all those old lineages of thought, how we might grow a network from scratch is very constructivist. You start with a single weight and a single input and output. Clearly you're not solving an XOR problem with that. Now we have a bunch of inputs, and you're still not solving an XOR problem.

items.question: How do you view the idea of a continually learning system using its own experience to change its network architecture?
items.object: Continual learning through changes to network architecture
items.answer: I think a system using its own learning experience to grow and change its architecture, in addition to its weights, in a continual sense, is a very interesting and exciting open problem. Luckily, people are thinking about it again.
quotes: Thinking about how a system can use its own learning experience to grow and change its architecture, in addition to its weights, in a continual sense, is a very interesting and exciting open problem.
Luckily, people are thinking about it again.

items.question: How do you think about the relationship between a person and their AI-enabled artificial limb?
items.object: The relationship between a person and their AI-enabled artificial limb
items.answer: We're really thinking about the interaction between a human, an artificial limb, and how artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies can allow someone to use an artificial limb to do all the things they want to do in their daily life. They're not limited by the technology; they want to express themselves and engage in their communities. They can do that. How do we use AI and machine learning to power that interaction? The view we take, and the view I've based my entire research line on, is in fact a very controversial one, I'd say: to consider the relationship between a person and their artificial limb as a multi-agent relationship. This is actually very contemporary because previously the sensors, actuators, and computation available sort of prohibited us from thinking about the machine part of that relationship as an agent. It wasn't able to build models of the person in any appreciable way or consider the environmental factors. With these surges in computational capacity and the ability of prostheses to be more like agents, we can now think about what it would mean to have a person and their bionic jointly acting in the world, working together to affect change in their shared environment in space and time. I think that's a really neat and different perspective.

items.question: How do you think the view of the brain as a continually refreshing system should inform how we think about digital systems?
items.object: The brain as a continually refreshing system and its relevance to digital systems
items.answer: We have left behind the thinking of the brain as a crystalline entity that slowly decays over time. We know there's new neurons created. We now know that it is a system that is continually refreshing itself. That's a big change in the neuroscience community over the last 50 years, and I think that's a nice way for us to consider how we might think about our digital systems as well.

rubrics.text: The response contrasts the brain’s continual renewal with the older view of the brain as a fixed structure that only deteriorates over time.

items.question: What do you find compelling about the Alberta Plan's ultimate goal?
items.object: The Alberta Plan's ultimate goal
items.answer: If you put those all together, you get a system. This is the end. It's a very simple one; it's right in the first paragraph of our manuscript: you get a system that can truly learn from its raw sensory motor experience and continue to do so over whatever its lifespan might be, in any environment—not even a human environment. I think that's a really beautiful thing to aspire to, and something that will help us more fundamentally understand the phenomenon of intelligence itself.
